Activities — Laptop and No-Laptop Tracks

Every activity in the class runs in two versions so nobody feels left out: one for people with a laptop in front of them, and one that needs nothing but a table, a partner, and these sheets. Merge the tracks at will — mixed tables often work best.

Activity 1 · 15 minutes · “Try it”

Laptop track: Your first real prompt

  1. Open a chat tool from the class demo (mix in tools a neighbor already trusts).
  2. Pick something real from your week: meal plan, trip idea, hard email, overdue chore.
  3. Write it using the recipe: role → context → ask. Example shape: “You are a friendly local guide. Planning a rainy afternoon with my 10-year-old niece who loves animals. Suggest 3 low-cost stops near downtown, plus one good indoor backup.”
  4. Read the reply as an editor: Is it right? Is it too long? Is it condescending? Would you say that?
  5. Change one thing and ask again — notice how small changes bend the answer.

No-laptop track: “Fix this prompt” pairs

  1. Partner up, take one card each (below), read the weak prompt aloud together.
  2. Fix it out loud in the recipe shape: role, context, clear ask.
  3. Make it good enough that either of you could paste it straight into a chat tool tonight.
  4. Swap cards and repeat. Two fixes each.
  5. Optional hard mode: keep the fix under 40 words.
Weak-prompt cards (cut apart before class):
  • “write me something about dogs”
  • “make my business better”
  • “what should I cook”
  • “help me learn Spanish”
  • “fix my resume”
  • “plan my day somehow”

Activity 2 · 10 minutes · “Real or fake?”

Both tracks together (works great even mixed)

  1. Groups of 2–3 get three messages (cards below, cut apart).
  2. Decide for each: real or fake?
  3. Then name the red flag that gave it away. Urgency? Odd payment? Self-proving link? Too-perfect story? Secrecy?
  4. Vote out loud per table. The disagreement is the lesson.

Laptop add-on: one-minute verification drill

After voting, the laptop half practices verifying separately: search the company’s name plus “customer service official site” in a fresh browser tab, and find the phone number the company itself publishes. Compare it to the one inside the message. Never click to verify — always swim upstream to shore.

Scam-message cards (cut apart; answer key on the last card)

Card A (“The Countdown”): “URGENT: Your email account will be closed in 24 hours. Click now to keep your files: bit-link.example/close-now”
Card B (“The Prize”): “Congratulations! You’ve won a $500 grocery gift card. Send a $1.50 processing fee and your card number, and we’ll ship it today!”
Card C (“The Visit”): “Hi, this is Maria from the county clerk’s office. We need to confirm your Medicare number for a paperwork renewal. Please call back at 555-0100 when you get a chance.”
Answer key: A = fake (urgency + self-proving link). B = fake (prize + odd payment + asks for card number). C = the tricky one: polite and unhurried — but government offices and Medicare never initiate calls like this, so treat it as fake until verified through the number on the official site. Every card has the same cure: pause, verify separately.
